claim: SWELL1 (LRRC8A) is the only essential subunit of the Volume Regulated Anion Channel (VRAC).
source: SWELL1 (LRRC8A) is the only essential subunit of the Volume Regulated Anion Channel (VRAC), which regulates cellular volume homeostasis and is activated by hypotonic solutions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about SWELL1/LRRC8A and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: VRAC regulates cellular volume homeostasis.
source: SWELL1 (LRRC8A) is the only essential subunit of the Volume Regulated Anion Channel (VRAC), which regulates cellular volume homeostasis and is activated by hypotonic solutions.
evidence: This is stated as an established function of VRAC in the abstract.

claim: VRAC is activated by hypotonic solutions.
source: SWELL1 (LRRC8A) is the only essential subunit of the Volume Regulated Anion Channel (VRAC), which regulates cellular volume homeostasis and is activated by hypotonic solutions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in the manuscript.

claim: SWELL1 together with four other LRRC8 family members potentially forms a vastly heterogeneous cohort of VRAC channels with different properties.
source: SWELL1, together with four other LRRC8 family members, potentially forms a vastly heterogeneous cohort of VRAC channels with different properties; however, SWELL1 alone is also functional.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction regarding heteromeric VRAC composition.

claim: SWELL1 alone is functional.
source: SWELL1, together with four other LRRC8 family members, potentially forms a vastly heterogeneous cohort of VRAC channels with different properties; however, SWELL1 alone is also functional.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing SWELL1 homomers can form functional channels.

claim: The structure of human homo-hexameric SWELL1 was determined at high resolution using cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Here, we report a high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structure of full-length human homo-hexameric SWELL1.
evidence: This is the primary finding reported in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the results section.

claim: SWELL1 has a trimer of dimers assembly.
source: The structure reveals a trimer of dimers assembly with symmetry mismatch between the pore-forming domain and the cytosolic leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in structural figures.

claim: There is symmetry mismatch between the pore-forming domain and the cytosolic leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domains in SWELL1.
source: The structure reveals a trimer of dimers assembly with symmetry mismatch between the pore-forming domain and the cytosolic leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: A charged residue at the narrowest constriction of the homomeric channel is an important pore determinant of heteromeric VRAC.
source: Importantly, mutational analysis demonstrates that a charged residue at the narrowest constriction of the homomeric channel is an important pore determinant of heteromeric VRAC.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mutational analysis data in Figure 4.

claim: A mutation in the flexible N-terminal portion of SWELL1 affects pore properties.
source: Additionally, a mutation in the flexible N-terminal portion of SWELL1 affects pore properties, suggesting a putative link between intracellular structures and channel regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data on T5 mutations in Figure 4.

claim: There is a putative link between intracellular structures and channel regulation in SWELL1.
source: Additionally, a mutation in the flexible N-terminal portion of SWELL1 affects pore properties, suggesting a putative link between intracellular structures and channel regulation.
evidence: This is suggested based on the observation that N-terminal mutations affect pore properties.

claim: VRAC is a ubiquitously expressed mammalian anion channel.
source: VRAC is a ubiquitously expressed mammalian anion channel implicated in diverse physiological processes including volume regulation, cell proliferation, release of excitatory amino acids, and apoptosis (Hyzinski-García et al., 2014; Nilius et al., 1997; Pedersen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: VRAC is implicated in volume regulation, cell proliferation, release of excitatory amino acids, and apoptosis.
source: VRAC is a ubiquitously expressed mammalian anion channel implicated in diverse physiological processes including volume regulation, cell proliferation, release of excitatory amino acids, and apoptosis (Hyzinski-García et al., 2014; Nilius et al., 1997; Pedersen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: VRAC is suggested to play a role in stroke, diabetes, and cancer.
source: It is suggested to play a role in a variety of human diseases including stroke, diabetes, and cancer (Hyzinski-García et al., 2014; Planells-Cases et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A chromosomal translocation in the SWELL1 (LRRC8A) gene is causatively linked to agammaglobulinemia, a human B cell deficiency disease.
source: A causative link has been established between a chromosomal translocation in the SWELL1 (LRRC8A) gene and a human B cell deficiency disease, agammaglobulinemia (Sawada et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: SWELL1 is required for VRAC activity.
source: Previous studies have shown that SWELL1 is required for VRAC activity, and that the presence of other LRRC8 subunits dictates functional characteristics of VRAC, including pore properties (Qiu et al., 2014; Syeda et al., 2016; Voss et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The presence of other LRRC8 subunits dictates functional characteristics of VRAC, including pore properties.
source: Previous studies have shown that SWELL1 is required for VRAC activity, and that the presence of other LRRC8 subunits dictates functional characteristics of VRAC, including pore properties (Qiu et al., 2014; Syeda et al., 2016; Voss et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SWELL1 and at least one other LRRC8 subunit are required for canonical whole-cell VRAC currents.
source: While SWELL1 and at least one other LRRC8 subunit are required for canonical whole-cell VRAC currents, purified homomers of SWELL1 reconstituted in lipid bilayers are activated by osmotic stimuli and blocked by VRAC antagonist, DCPIB (Syeda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Purified homomers of SWELL1 reconstituted in lipid bilayers are activated by osmotic stimuli.
source: While SWELL1 and at least one other LRRC8 subunit are required for canonical whole-cell VRAC currents, purified homomers of SWELL1 reconstituted in lipid bilayers are activated by osmotic stimuli and blocked by VRAC antagonist, DCPIB (Syeda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Purified homomers of SWELL1 reconstituted in lipid bilayers are blocked by VRAC antagonist DCPIB.
source: While SWELL1 and at least one other LRRC8 subunit are required for canonical whole-cell VRAC currents, purified homomers of SWELL1 reconstituted in lipid bilayers are activated by osmotic stimuli and blocked by VRAC antagonist, DCPIB (Syeda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: CRISPR-engineered HeLa cells lacking all LRRC8 subunits exhibited very small but significant DCPIB-sensitive hypotonicity-induced currents after SWELL1 overexpression.
source: Interestingly, CRISPR-engineered HeLa cells lacking all LRRC8 subunits (LRRC8-/- HeLa cells) exhibited very small but significant DCPIB-sensitive hypotonicity-induced currents after SWELL1 overexpression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), supporting previous bilayer results.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Human SWELL1-FLAG was recombinantly expressed in LRRC8(B,C,D,E)-/- HEK293-F suspension cells.
source: To produce homomeric SWELL1, human SWELL1-FLAG was recombinantly expressed in LRRC8(B,C,D,E)-/- HEK293-F suspension cells, then solubilized in 1% decyl maltose neopentyl glycol (DMNG) detergent, followed by purification and exchange into 0.05% digitonin for structure determination by cryo-EM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the methods used for structure determination.

claim: SWELL1 was solubilized in 1% decyl maltose neopentyl glycol (DMNG) detergent.
source: To produce homomeric SWELL1, human SWELL1-FLAG was recombinantly expressed in LRRC8(B,C,D,E)-/- HEK293-F suspension cells, then solubilized in 1% decyl maltose neopentyl glycol (DMNG) detergent, followed by purification and exchange into 0.05% digitonin for structure determination by cryo-EM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the methods used for structure determination.

claim: SWELL1 was exchanged into 0.05% digitonin for structure determination by cryo-EM.
source: To produce homomeric SWELL1, human SWELL1-FLAG was recombinantly expressed in LRRC8(B,C,D,E)-/- HEK293-F suspension cells, then solubilized in 1% decyl maltose neopentyl glycol (DMNG) detergent, followed by purification and exchange into 0.05% digitonin for structure determination by cryo-EM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the methods used for structure determination.

claim: Image analysis and reconstruction yielded a ~4 Å resolution map of SWELL1.
source: Image analysis and reconstruction yielded a ~4 Å resolution map that was used to build a molecular model of SWELL1 (Figure 1—figure supplements 3–4, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: SWELL1 is organized as a hexameric trimer of dimers.
source: SWELL1 is organized as a hexameric trimer of dimers with a four-layer domain architecture and an overall jellyfish-like shape (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SWELL1 has a four-layer domain architecture.
source: SWELL1 is organized as a hexameric trimer of dimers with a four-layer domain architecture and an overall jellyfish-like shape (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SWELL1 has an overall jellyfish-like shape.
source: SWELL1 is organized as a hexameric trimer of dimers with a four-layer domain architecture and an overall jellyfish-like shape (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The transmembrane (TM) and extracellular domains (ECDs) of SWELL1 surround the central pore axis.
source: The transmembrane (TM) and extracellular domains (ECDs) surround the central pore axis, and share a previously unappreciated structural homology with the connexin (Maeda et al., 2009) and innexin (Oshima et al., 2016) gap junction channels (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: SWELL1 shares a previously unappreciated structural homology with connexin and innexin gap junction channels.
source: The transmembrane (TM) and extracellular domains (ECDs) surround the central pore axis, and share a previously unappreciated structural homology with the connexin (Maeda et al., 2009) and innexin (Oshima et al., 2016) gap junction channels (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–D.

claim: The ECD of SWELL1 is composed of two extracellular loops (ECL1 and ECL2).
source: The ECD is composed of two extracellular loops (ECL1 and ECL2) that are stabilized by three disulfide bonds (Figure 1B–C and Figure 1—figure supplement 5E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in figures.

claim: The ECD of SWELL1 is stabilized by three disulfide bonds.
source: The ECD is composed of two extracellular loops (ECL1 and ECL2) that are stabilized by three disulfide bonds (Figure 1B–C and Figure 1—figure supplement 5E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in figures.

claim: ECL1 of SWELL1 contains one strand of a small beta-sheet and a helix (ECH) that faces the center of the ECD.
source: ECL1 contains one strand of a small beta-sheet and a helix (ECH) that faces the center of the ECD while ECL2 contains two additional antiparallel beta strands of the beta-sheet that faces the outside of the ECD.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the structural features.

claim: ECL2 of SWELL1 contains two additional antiparallel beta strands of the beta-sheet that faces the outside of the ECD.
source: ECL1 contains one strand of a small beta-sheet and a helix (ECH) that faces the center of the ECD while ECL2 contains two additional antiparallel beta strands of the beta-sheet that faces the outside of the ECD.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the structural features.

claim: Each subunit of SWELL1 contains four TM helices (TM1-4).
source: Each subunit contains four TM helices (TM1-4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the structural features.

claim: TM1 of SWELL1 lies closest to the central pore axis.
source: TM1 lies closest to the central pore axis and is tethered to a short N-terminal coil (NTC) that is parallel to the inner leaflet of the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the structural features.

claim: TM1 of SWELL1 is tethered to a short N-terminal coil (NTC) that is parallel to the inner leaflet of the membrane.
source: TM1 lies closest to the central pore axis and is tethered to a short N-terminal coil (NTC) that is parallel to the inner leaflet of the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the structural features.

claim: The intracellular linker domains (ILD) of SWELL1 create a tightly packed network of helices connecting the channel pore to the LRR domains.
source: In the cytosol, the intracellular linker domains (ILD) create a tightly packed network of helices connecting the channel pore to the LRR domains.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the structural features.

claim: Each ILD of SWELL1 is composed of two-four helices from the TM2-TM3 cytoplasmic loop (LH1-4), and five helices from the TM4-LRR linker (LH5-9).
source: Each ILD is composed of two-four helices from the TM2-TM3 cytoplasmic loop (LH1-4), and five helices from the TM4-LRR linker (LH5-9) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Each protomer of SWELL1 terminates in 15–16 LRRs which form a prototypical solenoid LRR fold.
source: Each protomer terminates in 15–16 LRRs which form a prototypical solenoid LRR fold (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in figures.

claim: LRRs from the six protomers of SWELL1 dimerize into three pairs, which interact to form a Celtic knot-like assembly.
source: LRRs from the six protomers dimerize into three pairs, which interact to form a Celtic knot-like assembly (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The ECDs, TMs, and ILDs of all six subunits of SWELL1 share the same 6-fold symmetric arrangement.
source: The ECDs, TMs, and ILDs all share the same 6-fold symmetric arrangement (Figure 2B); however, in the cytosol, LRR domains dimerize in a parallel fashion with each LRR at either a 10 or −20° offset relative to the rest of its protomer, producing a 3-fold symmetric trimer of dimers (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: LRR domains of SWELL1 dimerize in a parallel fashion with each LRR at either a 10 or −20° offset relative to the rest of its protomer, producing a 3-fold symmetric trimer of dimers.
source: The ECDs, TMs, and ILDs all share the same 6-fold symmetric arrangement (Figure 2B); however, in the cytosol, LRR domains dimerize in a parallel fashion with each LRR at either a 10 or −20° offset relative to the rest of its protomer, producing a 3-fold symmetric trimer of dimers (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The nonequivalence between identical subunits of SWELL1 arises from a hinge around the conserved residue L402 in a helix of the TM4-LRR linker.
source: The nonequivalence between identical subunits arises from a hinge around the conserved residue L402 in a helix of the TM4-LRR linker (Figure 2D and Figure 1—Figure supplements 6 and 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in figures.

claim: The hinge at L402 allows the LRR domains of SWELL1 to shift as rigid bodies.
source: This hinge allows the LRR domains to shift as rigid bodies, producing sufficient flexibility for them to interface at their edges via several charged residues (Figures 2D and 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in figures.

claim: The LRR domains of SWELL1 interface at their edges via several charged residues.
source: This hinge allows the LRR domains to shift as rigid bodies, producing sufficient flexibility for them to interface at their edges via several charged residues (Figures 2D and 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The helical C-termini of the two subunits in a dimer pair of SWELL1 make two different sets of interactions with the neighboring LRR.
source: As a result, the helical C-termini of the two subunits in a dimer pair make two different sets of interactions with the neighboring LRR (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Focused 3D classification of the LRR domains revealed several arrangements of LRRs suggesting that flexibility of the LRR domains may play a functional role in channel gating.
source: Focused 3D classification of the LRR domains revealed several arrangements of LRRs suggesting that flexibility of the LRR domains may play a functional role in channel gating (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), similar to the intracellular domains of the CorA magnesium channel (Matthies et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, with comparison to CorA cited.

claim: The outer LRR subunit in the dimer of SWELL1 exhibits helical density in the C-terminal half of the TM2-TM3 linker that rests on top of the outer protomer's LRR domain.
source: Interestingly, the outer LRR subunit in the dimer exhibits helical density in the C-terminal half of the TM2-TM3 linker that rests on top of the outer protomer's LRR domain, adding an additional layer of intricacy to the network of cytosolic interactions (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–B.

claim: Symmetry mismatch is observed in the homotetrameric AMPA receptor GluA2, which similarly forms local dimers in different domain layers.
source: Symmetry mismatch is also observed in the homotetrameric AMPA receptor GluA2, which similarly forms local dimers in different domain layers (Sobolevsky et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The dimer-of-dimers topology of homotetrameric AMPA-subtype ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) defines the subunit organization of di- and tri-heteromeric NMDA-subtype iGluR structures.
source: Furthermore, the dimer-of-dimers topology of homotetrameric AMPA-subtype ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) defines the subunit organization of di- and tri-heteromeric NMDA-subtype iGluR structures (Karakas and Furukawa, 2014; Lee et al., 2014; Lü et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The trimer-of-dimers assembly of SWELL1 is speculated to be recapitulated in, and influence the composition of, heteromeric VRACs.
source: By analogy, we speculate that the trimer-of-dimers assembly of SWELL1 is recapitulated in, and influences the composition of, heteromeric VRACs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as speculation based on analogy to iGluRs.

claim: There is little domain swapping between the subunits of the pore-forming domains of the SWELL1 channel.
source: Unlike other ion channels, there is little domain swapping between the subunits of the pore-forming domains of the SWELL1 channel.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from the structure.

claim: The individual helical bundles of SWELL1 are loosely packed with one another and lined with hydrophobic residues.
source: The individual helical bundles are loosely packed with one another and lined with hydrophobic residues.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from the structure.

claim: The inter-protomer space of SWELL1 may be occupied by hydrophobic membrane components like lipid or cholesterol that might be important for channel assembly or lipid signaling.
source: The inter-protomer space may be occupied by hydrophobic membrane components like lipid or cholesterol that might be important for channel assembly or lipid signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as speculation based on structural observations.

claim: Densities observed in the inter-subunit space in innexin-6 have been proposed to have a stabilizing role in the conformation of the helix bundles.
source: Such densities are observed in the inter-subunit space in innexin-6 and have been proposed to have a stabilizing role in the conformation of the helix bundles (Oshima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: A three residue KYD motif in SWELL1 was previously shown to be involved in voltage-dependent inactivation and selectivity.
source: At the upper faces of the extracellular domains, on mostly flexible loops, resides a three residue KYD motif previously shown to be involved in voltage-dependent inactivation and selectivity (Ullrich et al., 2016); interestingly, KYD extends laterally towards the neighboring subunit (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that subunit interactions in this region contribute to these channel properties.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The KYD motif of SWELL1 extends laterally towards the neighboring subunit, suggesting that subunit interactions in this region contribute to channel properties.
source: At the upper faces of the extracellular domains, on mostly flexible loops, resides a three residue KYD motif previously shown to be involved in voltage-dependent inactivation and selectivity (Ullrich et al., 2016); interestingly, KYD extends laterally towards the neighboring subunit (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that subunit interactions in this region contribute to these channel properties.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ECDs, TMs, and ILDs of all six subunits of SWELL1 contribute to the ion-conducting pore.
source: The ECDs, TMs, and ILDs of all six subunits contribute to the ion-conducting pore (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: Windows of 35 by 40 Å between LRR dimer pairs of SWELL1 are sufficiently large to allow ions and osmolytes to freely pass.
source: Below that, windows of 35 by 40 Å between LRR dimer pairs are sufficiently large to allow ions and osmolytes to freely pass.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on structural measurements.

claim: A ring of arginines (R103) at the N-terminal tip of the extracellular helix forms the narrowest constriction in the SWELL1 channel structure.
source: In the extracellular domain, 25 Å above the membrane, a ring of arginines (R103) at the N-terminal tip of the extracellular helix forms the narrowest constriction in the channel structure (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: R103 is only conserved between SWELL1 and the LRRC8B subunit (R99).
source: We hypothesized that these arginines, only conserved between SWELL1 and the LRRC8B subunit (R99) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), might directly interact with permeant anions.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The Vrev of currents mediated by SWELL1-R103F + LRRC8C was significantly reduced compared to wildtype channels, indicating that the channels are less selective for Cl-.
source: The Vrev of currents mediated by SWELL1-R103F + LRRC8C was significantly reduced compared to wildtype channels, indicating that the channels are less selective for Cl- (Figure 4D) (Ackerman et al., 1994; Jackson and Strange, 1995; Tsumura et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4D with supporting citations.

claim: Extracellular ATP at concentrations that block ~75% of wildtype VRAC currents was ineffective on channels containing R103F.
source: Furthermore, extracellular ATP at concentrations that block ~75% of wildtype VRAC currents was ineffective on channels containing R103F (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: R103 is a critical residue within SWELL1 that impacts ion selectivity as well as pore block of heteromeric VRAC channels.
source: Therefore, R103 is a critical residue within SWELL1 that impacts ion selectivity as well as pore block of heteromeric VRAC channels.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the mutational analysis data.

claim: Constrictions are observed at pore-facing residues T44 and T48 within the pore of SWELL1.
source: Within the pore, constrictions are observed at pore-facing residues T44 and T48 (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: Residue T44 was previously identified via the substituted cysteine accessibility method (SCAM) on heteromeric channels as likely to be at or near the pore.
source: Interestingly, we had previously identified residue T44 via the substituted cysteine accessibility method (SCAM) on heteromeric channels as likely to be at or near the pore (Qiu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: A constriction at the intracellular face of the membrane of SWELL1 corresponds to a short N-terminal coil (NTC) sitting parallel to the inner leaflet of the membrane.
source: Near the bottom of the pore cavity, a constriction at the intracellular face of the membrane corresponds to a short N-terminal coil (NTC) sitting parallel to the inner leaflet of the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from the structure.

claim: The first 14 residues of the N-terminus of SWELL1 are not resolved in the cryo-EM density, presumably due to flexibility.
source: The first 14 residues of the N-terminus of the channel are not resolved in the cryo-EM density, presumably due to flexibility.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from the structure.

claim: In the Cx26 and innexin-6 structures, an N-terminal helix forms a pore funnel structure that is the narrowest constriction in the structures of these channels and is thought to contribute to trafficking, selectivity, and gating.
source: The absence of these residues is conspicuous; in the Cx26 and innexin-6 structures, an N-terminal helix forms a pore funnel structure that is the narrowest constriction in the structures of these channels and is thought to contribute to trafficking, selectivity, and gating (Kyle et al., 2008; Maeda et al., 2009; Oshima, 2014; Oshima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The short portion of the NTC that is resolved in SWELL1 is highly coordinated by cytosolic domains and positioned to respond to conformational changes in the cytosolic domains of one protomer, as well as movements of the neighboring protomer.
source: In our reconstruction, the short portion of the NTC that is resolved is highly coordinated by cytosolic domains and positioned to respond to conformational changes in the cytosolic domains of one protomer, as well as movements of the neighboring protomer (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Whole-cell currents mediated by SWELL1-T5C + LRRC8C are strongly suppressed upon the addition of MTSES, suggesting that T5C is part of a constriction narrow enough to block the pore upon covalent modification by MTSES.
source: While MTSES has no effect on wildtype heteromeric channels (Qiu et al., 2014) or channels containing SWELL1-T5R (Figure 4G), whole-cell currents mediated by SWELL1-T5C + LRRC8C are strongly suppressed upon the addition of MTSES, suggesting that T5C is part of a constriction narrow enough to block the pore upon covalent modification by MTSES (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: SWELL1-T5R-containing channels are significantly more selective to iodide compared to chloride, confirming that this residue is close to or part of the channel pore.
source: Although SWELL1-T5C-containing channels have similar relative permeability to wildtype, SWELL1-T5R-containing channels are significantly more selective to iodide compared to chloride, confirming that this residue is close to or part of the channel pore (Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The unresolved portion of the N-terminus plays a role in pore constriction in native channels composed of SWELL1 and LRRC8C.
source: Thus, the unresolved portion of the N-terminus plays a role in pore constriction in native channels composed of SWELL1 and LRRC8C.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the T5 mutational analysis.

claim: The absence of the N-terminus in the SWELL1 structure is likely due to either the high flexibility of the region or a peculiarity of the homomeric assembly of the channel.
source: Its absence in our structure is likely due to either the high flexibility of the region or a peculiarity of the homomeric assembly of the channel.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as speculation about why the N-terminus is not resolved.

claim: Mutations based on the SWELL1 structure proved to be relevant for VRAC currents in a cellular context.
source: Electrophysiological analyses presented here demonstrate that the homomeric SWELL1 structure retains properties of more complex heteromers, as mutations based on the structure proved to be relevant for VRAC currents in a cellular context.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The homomeric SWELL1 structure retains properties of more complex heteromers.
source: Electrophysiological analyses presented here demonstrate that the homomeric SWELL1 structure retains properties of more complex heteromers, as mutations based on the structure proved to be relevant for VRAC currents in a cellular context.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Decreases in intracellular ionic strength cause activation of VRAC.
source: Since decreases in intracellular ionic strength cause activation (Syeda et al., 2016), gating would likely be initiated by movement of intracellular domains in response to changes in salt concentration.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Gating of VRAC would likely be initiated by movement of intracellular domains in response to changes in salt concentration.
source: Since decreases in intracellular ionic strength cause activation (Syeda et al., 2016), gating would likely be initiated by movement of intracellular domains in response to changes in salt concentration.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as speculation based on the structure and known activation mechanism.

claim: The multitude of charge-mediated interactions in the LRRs endows the SWELL1 structure with ionic-strength sensitivity.
source: We speculate that the multitude of charge-mediated interactions in the LRRs endows the SWELL1 structure with ionic-strength sensitivity, and via interactions with the N-terminus, the ILDs couple LRR movement to the transmembrane channel.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as speculation based on the structural observations.

claim: Via interactions with the N-terminus, the ILDs couple LRR movement to the transmembrane channel.
source: We speculate that the multitude of charge-mediated interactions in the LRRs endows the SWELL1 structure with ionic-strength sensitivity, and via interactions with the N-terminus, the ILDs couple LRR movement to the transmembrane channel.
